title: Marlin Ops — Context Length, Tool-Calling & Deployment Pathways
summary: Initial discovery with Marlin Ops about selecting inference deployment (hosted/dedicated/private) and model choices for a multi-tenant logistics platform. Key concerns: long-context handling for shipment histories, multilingual generation (EN/ES/PT), function/tool-calling for structured lookup (shipment status, pricing), data residency and auditability. Redwood AE+SE discussed options, rough perf expectations, and next steps for a pilot including benchmarks and security docs.
next_steps: Redwood to share Dedicated pricing + quick TCO sketch (Rachel)
SE to run 2 sample benchmarks (1 short-latency, 1 long-context) against Marlin sample prompts (Diego)
Customer to provide redacted sample conversation logs and tool API spec (Jon/Marcus)
action_items: Rachel: Send Dedicated vs Hosted comparison and estimated monthly cost (due 2027-10-01)
Diego: Run 2 benchmarks (8k context + 64k context) on candidate open models and share perf/cost spreadsheet (due 2027-09-29)
Jon: Share sanitized chat transcripts and core tool endpoints for tool-calling test (due 2027-09-28)
Marcus: Confirm VPC networking constraints and whether on-prem is required (due 2027-09-30)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-25
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Rachel Kim (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Redwood Solutions), Anika Patel (Marlin CTO), Jon Reyes (Marlin Head of ML), Marcus Li (Marlin Infra), Sofia Duarte (Marlin PM)

[00:00] Rachel Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. I'm Rachel from Redwood, AE on this account. With me is Diego, our systems engineer, and Priya on solutions. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Anika Patel: Doing well, thanks. Appreciate you carving time. We're at a point where we need to pick a path for inference — trying to understand tradeoffs between hosted, dedicated, and our private options.
[00:14] Rachel Kim: Totally. Can you give a quick overview of the product surface and the key constraints you're seeing?
[00:19] Sofia Duarte: Sure. Marlin Ops runs a logistics coordination platform — lots of multi-turn chat between dispatchers and drivers, plus programmatic lookups into pricing and shipment history. We need generation and tool-calling. Also, we need Spanish and Portuguese support for LATAM markets.
[00:29] Jon Reyes: Add to that: we have very long context needs sometimes — customers will paste weeks of conversation and manifests. We might need 32k, 64k, or even 128k tokens in some flows. Latency matters for live chat (target < 800ms ideally for short responses), but some batch summary tasks can accept higher latency.
[00:45] Diego Alvarez: That's helpful. Quick clarifying Q: when you say 128k context, is that full attention across all tokens, or are you considering retrieval + condensed context?
[00:53] Jon Reyes: Both. For summaries we want full context. For routing and quick lookups we can do retrieval + short prompt. But we want the option to run generation across long windows occasionally.
[01:02] Rachel Kim: Understood. On the deployment side, what are your data residency/audit constraints? Any requirement for on-prem or VPC-only?
[01:08] Marcus Li: We need audit logs and integration with our KMS for key rotation. Ideally, we'd prefer VPC with private connectivity to our APIs. On-prem is an option but adds ops overhead. SOC2 compliance is a must for customers.
[01:17] Priya Shah: Redwood Private supports a customer-controlled control plane and KMS/HSM integrations, and Dedicated gives reserved capacity with VPC peering options — so there's flexibility. Diego, maybe you want to talk about performance profiles across models?
[01:28] Diego Alvarez: Sure. From a model perspective we usually separate candidate families: large open decoder-only (Llama-like), encoder-decoder hybrids, and some LLMs with specialized long-context kernels. For 32k we have good options with quantized variants; for 64k and 128k we often recommend models that have optimizations for sliding window attention or chunked attention. There are tradeoffs: longer context models can have higher per-token cost and latency.
[01:51] Anika Patel: Do you have specific model names you recommend for multilingual and tool-calling? We've seen mixed behavior with in-house fine-tuned models and OpenAI endpoints.
[01:58] Diego Alvarez: For multilingual we typically look at models that were trained on diverse corpora — some Llama-derivs, Mistral multilingual branches, and specialized opt-followups. For tool-calling, function-calling support is mostly an inference-time pattern. We can run structured output with constrained decoding or a tool-layer that maps tokens to tool invocations. Redwood supports function/tool calling patterns in the hosted API, and the same interface is available on Dedicated/Private.
[02:24] Jon Reyes: When you say 'tool layer', do you mean Redwood handles the orchestration or we need to build a middleware?
[02:29] Diego Alvarez: Preferably you implement the business logic for tool side-effects, but Redwood provides structured output helpers, streaming, and safety hooks. For example, you can declare a JSON schema for the tool input and the model can be constrained to produce that. We also have examples of a function-calling shim. A few customers use our built-in retriever + tool integration.
[02:48] Marcus Li: I'm worried about KV cache and memory blowups with huge contexts. How does Redwood manage KV cache and memory when working with 64k+?
[02:55] Diego Alvarez: Good question. Our runtime manages KV cache and can shard across GPUs; for extremely long contexts we use chunked attention or windowed KV caching. For Dedicated we can provision larger GPU pools or NVLink clusters. For Private on-prem you can size machines accordingly but need to plan for OOM patterns. We'll capture memory-per-token profiles in the benchmark.
[03:15] Sofia Duarte: We also have budget constraints. Do you have rough cost multipliers for long-context models vs standard 8k?
[03:21] Rachel Kim: Ballpark: per-token compute and memory increase linearly with context in many runtimes, but optimized kernels and quantization can reduce costs. For a very rough estimate, 64k might be 4-6x cost of 8k for end-to-end generation depending on batching. Diego will provide more precise numbers after the benchmarks.
[03:39] Anika Patel: How about latency — if we need interactive chat with 1-turn short responses but sometimes append 32k of history, what's the typical pattern?
[03:46] Diego Alvarez: Many teams use a hybrid: keep short-window conversational state (2-4k) for immediate responses and run background jobs for long-context summarization or retrieval. For cases where long-history must be included synchronously, expect higher latency; we'd recommend Dedicated with pinned model variants to meet SLOs.
[04:04] Jon Reyes: We also use few-shot examples heavily — does Redwood make prompt templating and evals easy?
[04:09] Priya Shah: Redwood Console has prompt sets, regression alerts, and eval harnesses. You can pin prompt sets to rollout policies to catch quality regressions during model or quantization changes.
[04:17] Sofia Duarte: That would help. Our product folks need to iterate prompts a lot.
[04:21] Anika Patel: I want to dig deeper on security. SOC2 and SAML SSO are non-negotiable. Does your hosted product meet SOC2 and provide SSO + audit logs?
[04:30] Rachel Kim: Our hosted API is SOC2 compliant, supports SAML/SSO for the console, and we provide audit logs and token-level tracing. For stricter controls we can offer Dedicated with network isolation or Private with customer control plane and KMS/HSM integration.
[04:45] Marcus Li: If we go Dedicated, how isolated is the data? Is there a risk of cross-tenant caching?
[04:50] Diego Alvarez: Dedicated capacity isolates customer workloads at the GPU pool level, and we avoid shared KV caches across tenants. For absolute isolation, Private gives you full control. We can include details about zero cross-tenant KV policies in the security docs we'll share.
[05:04] Jon Reyes: About model life-cycle — how do rollouts and fallback work? If a new quantized variant drops quality, can we auto-fallback to a previous model?
[05:11] Rachel Kim: Yes. Rollouts support canary and A/B, and automatic fallback to pinned model versions on quality or latency regressions. Console exposes per-model quality metrics and you can set thresholds to trigger rollbacks.
[05:21] Sofia Duarte: Great — that addresses a lot. Can we talk about pilot scope and timeline? We're hoping to have a POC within 3-4 weeks.
[05:28] Rachel Kim: That's feasible. Typical pilot: we run perf and quality benchmarks on 2 candidate models, set up a small Dedicated pool or a Private eval deployment, run tool-calling flows against your sanitized endpoints, and evaluate costs. Diego: what do you need from Marlin to start?
[05:39] Diego Alvarez: We need 3 things: a) a representative set of prompts/transcripts (sanitized), b) API specs for the tool calls (endpoints, auth, request/response shapes), and c) a few quality metrics you care about (ROUGE, exact match on structured outputs, subjective fluency). With that we can run the 8k vs 32k vs 64k tests and provide latency/cost per-call numbers.
[06:02] Jon Reyes: We'll send those. One tricky ask: sometimes we need to call internal microservices for realtime pricing. Can Redwood's function-calling pattern support auth headers and ephemeral tokens?
[06:12] Diego Alvarez: The Redwood function-calling shim just returns structured output; your middleware is responsible for signing requests. That said, for Private we can run middleware inside your network so the flow doesn't traverse public internet. For Hosted/Dedicated we support VPC peering and private link to reduce exposure.
[06:29] Marcus Li: Any gotchas with GPU types? For 64k contexts do you recommend A100 style memory or new HBM GPUs?
[06:36] Diego Alvarez: For long contexts, memory bandwidth and larger HBM are beneficial — A100/RTX-A5000 or equivalent are common. Some customers use clustered GPUs with NVLink to handle larger KV caches. We'll include recommended instance types in the benchmark report.
[06:51] Rachel Kim: On the model choice side, would you prefer to start with an open model baseline or test a managed vendor first?
[06:57] Jon Reyes: We'd prefer open models to avoid vendor lock-in and for better control over behavior. However, if a managed model clearly outperforms on cost or latency, we might consider it.
[07:06] Diego Alvarez: Perfect. We'll test a couple of open models — one with strong multilingual behavior and one optimized for long context. We'll also include a managed baseline for reference.
[07:15] Sofia Duarte: A question on embeddings: we use embeddings for retrieval; if we host embeddings in-house vs Redwood embeddings, what's the tradeoff?
[07:22] Priya Shah: You can host your embeddings and build your retriever. Redwood can store and serve embeddings as part of the pipeline; dedicated storage options exist. Tradeoffs are latency and maintenance vs simplicity. We'll surface options in the TCO.
[07:37] Anika Patel: Regarding monitoring, can we get token-level cost breakdowns mapped to routes/teams? We want visibility per feature (chat vs summary).
[07:45] Rachel Kim: Yes — Console shows token-level breakdowns by route, model, and token type. You can also tag routes to teams for chargeback.
[07:53] Jon Reyes: Are there any limits on function-calling rate or concurrency? We expect bursts during peak scheduling windows.
[07:59] Diego Alvarez: We have rate-limits configurable per-customer. Dedicated capacity gives you headroom and predictable throughput; autoscaling policies can be configured to handle bursts. We'll capture expected concurrency numbers in the pilot plan.
[08:12] Marcus Li: About SSO: can we integrate SAML with our Okta?
[08:16] Rachel Kim: Yes. We support SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning for user sync. For Private you can federate to your identity provider directly.
[08:24] Sofia Duarte: Any customer references in logistics?
[08:27] Rachel Kim: We have a couple of logistics customers doing similar long-context routing; happy to share anonymized case studies once we get your NDA in place.
[08:34] Anika Patel: Let's talk specifics for the benchmark. Diego, can you outline the test matrix you'll run?
[08:40] Diego Alvarez: We'll run: (1) 8k context latency and cost test for typical chat (50 requests at concurrent 4), (2) 32k full-attention generation (20 requests concurrent 2), (3) 64k chunked attention pass (10 requests serial), (4) tool-calling flow test with structured output validation, (5) multilingual QA in EN/ES/PT for quality scoring. We'll run each on 2 open models and one managed baseline.
[09:03] Jon Reyes: For the multilingual test, include business Spanish and Portuguese idioms if possible.
[09:08] Diego Alvarez: Will do.
[09:09] Rachel Kim: Timeline: Diego aims to have results by 2027-09-29. We'll also send Dedicated pricing and a short TCO by 2027-10-01. Does that align with your internal timeline?
[09:18] Marcus Li: Yes. We'll aim to review internally and kick off a pilot second week of October.
[09:24] Sofia Duarte: A couple more quick technical Qs — how do you handle latency-sensitive streams? We want server-sent events style streaming to the UI.
[09:32] Priya Shah: Redwood supports streaming via the API with chunked responses and a websocket/streaming SDK pattern. We also support partial function-calling emissions so you can act on tool calls mid-stream.
[09:44] Anika Patel: If there are quality regressions post-quantization, is there an easy rollback path? We heard about hallucination regression with quantized weights in other setups.
[09:52] Diego Alvarez: That's why our Optimize product suggests quantization profiles with evals. You can pin to a float model while trialing quantized ones or route a percentage of traffic to each model. If quality drops beyond thresholds we auto-fallback based on your policies.
[10:06] Jon Reyes: Any legal/procurement needs on our side to get security docs?
[10:10] Rachel Kim: We'll share the security bundle (SOC2 report, penetration test summary, network topology options) after the NDA. I'll attach that in the follow-up.
[10:19] Sofia Duarte: Sounds good. Do you have a recommended success criteria for the pilot? We want clear pass/fail gates.
[10:25] Priya Shah: Suggested: (1) latency SLOs met for interactive flows (p95 < 800ms for short responses), (2) structured tool-call accuracy > 95% on validated schema tests, (3) per-call cost within X% of TCO target, and (4) no security blockers for VPC/KMS. We can refine those with Marlin.
[10:44] Anika Patel: That helps. One last operational question: who owns the model updates if we start with open models? Do we rely on Redwood upgrades or do we manage versions?
[10:52] Diego Alvarez: You can pin model versions and roll them through Redwood Console. We handle underlying runtime optimizations and quantization builds, but you control which versions are live. If you want to bring a custom fine-tuned model, we can host that on Dedicated or Private and respect your version tags.
[11:06] Rachel Kim: Great. I'll recap next steps: Rachel will send pricing/TCO and the security bundle; Diego will run the benchmarks and share spreadsheets; Jon/Marcus will provide sanitized transcripts and tool API specs; we'll aim to have pilot kickoff in mid-October. Any additions?
[11:20] Jon Reyes: No, that's good. Thanks — excited to see the numbers.
[11:24] Anika Patel: Thanks everyone.
[11:26] Rachel Kim: Thanks all, we'll follow up with calendar invites and the docs.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription: minor name mismatches possible; tool names and product lines abbreviated. Some disfluency preserved.
